messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 31
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Social Media Manager
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Vignette:
Nadia Khalil is a 31-year-old Lebanese-American woman who works as a social media manager for a mid-sized lifestyle brand. She presents for her first course of trauma-focused therapy approximately fourteen months after an incident that she describes, with considerable difficulty, as the worst thing she has ever done. She was driving home from a colleague's birthday dinner on a wet November evening, sober but tired, when she made a left turn through what she had judged to be a clear intersection and struck a cyclist who had been riding without lights in her blind spot. The impact was immediate and disorienting — the sound of it, a dense, hollow thud against the front quarter panel, and then the smell: rain on hot asphalt, and something metallic she later understood to be blood. The cyclist, a man in his forties, survived but sustained a severe traumatic brain injury and has required ongoing care. Nadia stayed at the scene, called 911, and knelt beside him in the road until the paramedics arrived. She was not charged with any offence. None of that, she has said, makes any difference to her.

In the weeks that followed, Nadia found herself unable to articulate what had happened to almost anyone. She would open her mouth to explain it to her mother or to a friend and discover that the words simply were not there — not the right ones, not any ones. She could hold the facts of the event in her mind like objects in a sealed box, but language would not reach them. At other times the opposite would happen: she would be sitting at her desk scheduling posts for the brand's Instagram account, and the smell would arrive without warning — that same wet-metal-asphalt combination — and for a moment she would be back in the intersection, kneeling on the road. These moments arrived without any clear trigger she could name, and they left her shaken and disoriented in ways she found hard to justify to herself or to her colleagues.

What frightened Nadia most, in the months that accumulated after the accident, was not the memory itself but what she had concluded about herself from it. She had come to believe, with a certainty that felt irrefutable, that she could not be trusted to do the right thing in any situation that mattered. She had thought she was a careful driver. She had thought she was a responsible person. The accident had, in her view, exposed something fundamental about her judgment that could not now be unseen. When a colleague placed a hand on her shoulder to look at her screen, Nadia would flinch sharply, her whole body registering danger before her mind had time to assess the situation. She would apologise and laugh it off, but privately she was certain that something in her had been permanently altered — that the woman she had been before November no longer existed, and that what remained was someone she did not recognise and was not sure she wanted to know.

Her marriage, already under strain, ended six months after the accident. She does not describe the divorce as a consequence of the trauma so much as another piece of evidence that she is not who she thought she was. She stopped attending the monthly dinners her Lebanese community group holds, partly because the drive across town in the dark felt impossible, and partly because she could not bear to sit with people who remembered the version of her that predated all of this. Her world has grown considerably smaller.

She continues to work, though the job has become its own kind of difficulty. Managing the brand's cheerful, aspirational content while cycling through episodes of strong, formless guilt and shame that arrive without apparent warning has left her feeling fraudulent in a way she cannot fully describe. On days when a near-miss notification or a breaking-news alert triggers a sudden sense of alarm — her body convinced, briefly, that something terrible is about to happen — she has learned to close her office door and wait for it to pass.

What finally brought Nadia to seek help was a conversation with her younger sister, who told her plainly that she seemed to have disappeared. Nadia could not argue with that. What she hopes for, she says carefully, is to recognise herself again. What she is most afraid of is that there is nothing left to recognise.
